8.layer4_ar: يتمتع تفسير هذه الآية على أنها تُقرُّ بكمال عدل الله بإجماع تام عبر جميع التراثات الإسلامية. ويُبيِّن علماء السنة كابن كثير والطبري والقرطبي أن هذا السؤال البلاغي يستدعي جواباً بـ"نعم" وأنه يُثبت أن الله منتهى الحكمة والعدل. ويُقرُّ التراثان الشيعي والسني بأن هذه صفةٌ جوهرية لله، فهو عدلٌ لا يظلم أحداً ولا يُضيِّع عملاً صالحاً. ويستعرض الرازي الأبعاد الكلامية لهذه الصفة، مُبيِّناً أن عدل الله لا ينفصل عن سائر صفاته من العلم والحكمة والقدرة. والفهم المشترك أن هذه الآية تُبعث الطمأنينة بالمساءلة والعدل الإلهي، وهو ركنٌ في عقيدة الإسلام. ومحل الاختلاف ينصبُّ على الممارسة في الغالب؛ إذ يتضمن التراث الشيعي استجابةً تأكيدية محددة عند تلاوة هذه الآية، بينما لا يشتمل التراث السني بالضرورة على هذه العادة بعينها وإن كانت الموافقة على مضمونها موصولة غير مقطوعة. ويُوظِّف كلا التراثين هذه الآية خاتمةً لبحوث العدل الإلهي والبعث والمساءلة. والرسالة إنسانية وعصرية في آنٍ: الله القاضي الأعلى وحكمه بالغ العدل لا تشوبه شائبة.
8.layer1: The surah closes with one of the Quran's most majestic rhetorical questions: 'Is Allah not the most just of judges?' The Arabic a-laysa Allahu bi-ahkami al-hakimin ends the surah on a note of absolute certainty and awe, inviting the reader to acknowledge what cannot be reasonably denied. The word hakimin here is the plural of hakim, meaning judge or one who judges wisely, and the superlative ahkam means the most precise, the most just, the most capable in judgment. Allah is declared to be not merely a just judge but the very standard of justice against which all other judgments are measured. This closing question serves multiple functions in the surah. It confirms that the reversal promised in verse five — the reduction of the heedless person to the lowest of the low — is an act of perfect justice, not arbitrary punishment. It also confirms that the reward promised in verse six — the uninterrupted recompense for believers — is an act of perfect justice, not favouritism or whim. Above all, it challenges every listener to reflect on their own conduct: if the most just of judges will call us to account, how should we live? The recommended response from the Prophet, preserved in authentic hadith, is to say 'Bala wa ana ala dhalika min al-shahidin' — Yes, and I am among those who witness to it. This makes the recitation of the surah an act of renewing one's testimony to divine justice and one's commitment to living accountably.
8.layer2: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim comments that this closing verse encapsulates the theological foundation of all that has preceded it. He cites the hadith recorded by Ahmad, Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim, and Ibn Marduwayh on the authority of Abu Hurayra that the Prophet said: 'When one of you recites Surah Wat-tin waz-zaytun and reaches alaysa Allahu bi-ahkami al-hakimin, he should say: Bala wa ana ala dhalika min al-shahidin.' This prophetic instruction transforms the verse from a purely declarative statement into a moment of active personal testimony. Tabari in Jami al-Bayan explains that ahkam al-hakimin means the most perfect in judgment, the One whose decrees are characterised by absolute equity, comprehensive knowledge, and infinite wisdom — attributes that no human judge can fully claim. Qurtubi in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran draws a theological conclusion from this verse: divine justice requires the Day of Resurrection, because much injustice in this world goes without correction. The Quran's insistence that Allah is the most just of judges is therefore a promise that all wrongdoing will be addressed, all oppression will be answered, and all sincere virtue will be honoured. This is why denying the Day of Recompense, as challenged in the preceding verse, is ultimately a denial of divine justice itself. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi observes that the rhetorical question form of this verse — a-laysa (Is He not?) — is an expression of certainty so overwhelming that it invites assent rather than debate, making the surah conclude on the strongest possible note of affirmation.
8.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes the closing of Surah At-Tin as a breathtaking act of divine rhetoric: the surah opened with majestic oaths calling creation to witness, proceeded to declare the glory and tragedy of human nature, and closes by unveiling the ultimate guarantee behind everything — the perfect, unassailable justice of Allah. Qutb writes that for the believer who has truly absorbed the surah's journey, this closing question does not feel like a challenge but like a relief, a resting point of absolute certainty that whatever happens in the confusion and apparent injustice of the world, the final word belongs to the most just of all judges. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir emphasises the practical implication of this verse for Muslim communities: those who believe in Allah as ahkam al-hakimin must themselves aspire to justice in their personal dealings, social institutions, and governance structures. A community that proclaims this verse in prayer but tolerates systemic injustice in its own ranks has not truly internalised its meaning. Ibn Uthaymeen highlighted the recommended prophetic response when reciting this verse, noting that the formula 'Bala wa ana ala dhalika min al-shahidin' is an act of verbal worship that anchors the reciter's heart to the conviction of divine accountability. In an age when justice systems are widely perceived as fallible, biased, and incomplete, the Quranic declaration that there exists a Judge who is the most just of all judges offers a profound source of spiritual stability, ethical motivation, and ultimate hope for all who have been wronged and await the only tribunal where perfect justice will be served.
